thread.title: Sceye partners with NASA and USGS on high-altitude environmental monitoring
thread.title_full: Sceye partners with NASA and USGS on high-altitude environmental monitoring

author: New Mexico Sun
title: Sceye partners with NASA and USGS on high-altitude environmental monitoring
text:
Sceye, a company based in New Mexico, is working on a new type of high-altitude aircraft designed to monitor environmental events from the stratosphere. The company recently announced a partnership with NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) for projects involving environmental monitoring, imaging, and data collection.
The company's High-Altitude Platform System (HAPS) is an unmanned vessel filled with helium that operates above 60,000 feet in the Earth's stratosphere. Sceye says this altitude allows for closer observation than satellites in low-Earth or geosynchronous orbit, making it possible to capture high-resolution images of methane emissions and other phenomena.
“We can see methane with a granularity of less than one meter pixel, and that allows us to see the specific emitter,” said Sceye founder and CEO Mikkel Vestergaard Frandsen. “Because we’re station keeping, we can quantify the rate of emission. We can do that in real-time.”
Sceye's collaboration with NASA and USGS comes after successful test launches of its system. In September, the company completed a Series C funding round that brought its total funding to over $200 million.
Although Sceye aims for its HAPS to remain in the stratosphere for extended periods—potentially months or years—the longest flight so far has lasted just over 24 hours. The aircraft uses solar panels during daylight hours and battery power at night. Mission control staff currently oversee launches and flights, but Sceye plans to increase automation in future operations.
“Next year’s flight program is about endurance, just staying up as long as possible, staying up to see what fails first,” Vestergaard Frandsen said. “And while we do so, also softly introduce commercialization.”
While detecting methane leaks is one application for Sceye's technology—methane being a greenhouse gas significantly more potent than carbon dioxide—the aircraft can also carry different payloads for various uses such as early wildfire detection or monitoring extreme weather and earthquakes.
“We’re quite focused on the climate aspects of what we as an aerospace company can do,” Vestergaard Frandsen added.
